 5.) Over-broad & Unanswerable Referral Question

 Axiomatic in professional assessment is that the referral question organizes the assessment procedures. The psychometrics underlying assessment are based on probability and statistics. An over-broad and unfocused referral question (such as “What’s wrong with Johnny?”) leads to the collection of large amounts of information in a wide range of domains that statistically raise the probability of spurious findings based on statistical probability alone (associations in the data that are just chance associations).

on statistical probability alone (associations in the data that are just chance associations). A more focused referral question, on the other hand (such as, “Does Johnny have autism?”), limits the scope of data collection to the information necessary to answer the referral question, thereby limiting the probability of obtaining spurious associations based on chance.

 Child custody evaluations seek to answer the referral question, “What should the child’s custody visitation schedule be?”  This is an overbroad referral question that results in the unfocused collection of family history information. Spurious associations will occur in the information simply as a result of the over-extended collection of data and the psychometric context created by an over-broad referral question.

collection of data and the psychometric context created by an over-broad referral question.

 In clinical psychology, when an over-broad referral question is initially offered by the client, clinical psychologists (who are knowledgeable in assessment) work with the client to develop a more appropriate limited-scope referral question. In court-involved family conflict surrounding attachment-related family pathology following divorce, I would propose that a more professionally responsible referral question for assessment is:

 Limited Scope Referral Question: “Which parent is the source of pathogenic parenting creating the child’s attachment-related family pathology surrounding divorce, and what are the treatment implications?”

family pathology surrounding divorce, and what are the treatment implications?”

 This more limited scope referral question avoids having to operationally define the “best interests” of the child and provides the structure necessary for a structured and limited-scope assessment of pathology (that substantially reduces the financial costs of the assessment, making the benefits from professional psychology accessible to all families, including lower-income families).

 A Limited Scope Assessment Protocol

 6.) Cultural and Personal Bias

 The practice of child custody evaluations is highly vulnerable to cultural and personal bias. Personal bias would enter the assessment through the evaluator’s own unresolved family of origin issues (counter-transference).

assessment through the evaluator’s own unresolved family of origin issues (counter-transference). Cultural bias would similarly enter the assessment process through the evaluator’s own cultural context for interpreting the data.

 While some may argue that personal bias can be eliminated by self-awareness (not a position I would take), cultural bias is absolutely present in the evaluator’s assessment. Everything we do as psychologists is embedded within a historical and cultural context. This is established foundational knowledge of cultural psychology. The child custody evaluator will be influenced by this evaluator’s historical and cultural context. That is a fact established by the field of cultural psychology.

historical and cultural context. That is a fact established by the field of cultural psychology.

 The issue is not whether the historical and cultural context is influencing the custody evaluator, the issue is limiting the bias inherent to the assessment process against cultural value systems that differ from the White Protestant Northern-European values of the surrounding culture in the United States, and from the culturally embedded personal beliefs and values of the individual custody evaluator.

 The more latitude the evaluator is allowed regarding the interpretation of the evaluation data, the greater the potential for unconscious personal and cultural bias to enter the conclusions and recommendations reached by the evaluator.

personal and cultural bias to enter the conclusions and recommendations reached by the evaluator. Both personal and cultural bias in assessment can be substantially limited the more structured the assessment protocol becomes.

 What specific steps do child custody evaluations take to limit the personal and cultural bias of the evaluator? None. Guidelines can encourage evaluators to refrain from bias due to personal or cultural beliefs, but these Guidelines have no practical impact on the actual conduct of any individual custody evaluation. Custody evaluations are conducted by one person and the reports are typically sealed by the court.

of the data, the conclusions reached, and the recommendations made, is never revealed.

 There exist NO structural safeguards with the child custody evaluation protocol to limit the impact of personal and cultural bias on the interpretation of family data, on the conclusions reached, and on the recommendations made in child custody evaluations, and to the degree that there are no guidelines specific to how designated principles and constructs of professional psychology are to be applied to interpret the child custody data (identification of relevance and weighting), child custody evaluators are allowed to apply, not apply, or misapply, any, some, or none of the constructs and principles of professional psychology.

apply, or misapply, any, some, or none of the constructs and principles of professional psychology. This is exactly the type of arbitrary assessment procedure that becomes extremely vulnerable to the introduction of personal and cultural bias into the interpretation of data.

The Parenting Practices Rating Scale is designed to document the clinical assessment of parenting by the targeted parent. The scale contains four primary items:

 1.)  Category Level of Parenting:

 Item 1, the Category Level of Parenting, identifies deviant-abusive parenting relative to broadly normal-range parenting.

 The Level of parenting is rated on a 4-point Likert scale (abusive, severely problematic, normal-range problematic, normal-range healthy), anchored by descriptive categories of parenting. Identifying the category of parenting locates the parenting in the corresponding Level of the rating scale.

 The 4-point Likert scale is then brought together into two broad categories of parenting; deviant-abusive (Levels 1 and 2) and normal-range (Levels 3 and 4).

 The structure of the family of origin is less important than the degree of conflict in the family of origin. High conflict families of origin can undermine the person’s ability to recognize and use effective problem-solving skills for conflict resolution because this person never had these problem resolution skills modeled by parents during childhood development.

 That’s the structural backbone of a written treatment plan.

 What is the goal to be achieved by therapy (Objectives)?

 How are you going to achieve those goals (Clinical Interventions)?

 I’ll go into each of these areas in a moment, but before leaving the form I want to point out a couple of other important features of a written treatment plan demonstrated by this county form.

Those time-frames are typically considered the standard of practice review points for treatment plans. Treatment goals should typically be for a three- to six-month range for resolution of the pathology. Short-term goals in the four- to six-week range are helpful progress milestones toward achieving the longer 3 to 6-month solutions.

Remember, the treatment objectives are identified in ways that are “measurable” and “time-bound” – permitting review of goal accomplishment.

 Instrument: PC-RRS

 The three items rated on the PC-RRS (Affection, Cooperation, and Social Involvement) are rated on a 7-point Likert scale from problematic (1s and 2s) to exceptionally positive (6s and 7s). The Affection scale monitors parent-child attachment bonding. The Cooperation scale monitors emotional disruptions (emotional flexibility and inflexibility). The Social Involvement scale monitors arousal emotions (anxiety, stress, sadness, and depression).

 The items are structured to reflect a normal-curve distribution, with normal-range being a middle rating of 4, extremely problematic behavior is rated a 1, and highly favorable behavior is rated a 7.  There was testimony in opposition to the legislation. The opposition arguments were all offered from legal professionals. The committee did not hear from any representatives from clinical psychology and family therapy. Screening questions, assessment tools, and interview frameworks are directed entirely toward identifying one parent as IPV victim and the other as perpetrator based on allegations of physical and coercive control violence. No assessment framework is provided for evaluating whether the child’s rejection is authentic or induced, whether the allied parent’s conduct meets criteria for psychological child abuse, or whether the targeted parent is the actual IPV victim.

 3.04: The harm potential from this omission is severe and specific. Targeted parents — who in Path B/Path C cases are the actual IPV victims — will be identified as abusers.

 This module requires the addition of a discrete section on the differential diagnosis of child rejection of a parent in IPV-allegation cases, organized around the three-pathway model described above, incorporating DSM-5 V995.82 and V995.51, and including specific assessment guidance for evaluating the possibility that the allied parent is the IPV perpetrator and the child’s induced pathology is the abuse weapon.

Patterns of Pathology
There are two primary patterns evidenced by the allied parent. These
patterns tend to have a gender association, although not always. Narcissistic Dad & Normal-Range Mom
One common pattern-type is a narcissistic father (Dark Triad & Dark
Tetrad) and a normal-range mother. This is the “bad mommy” pattern
and tends to have a higher spousal abuse orientation to it. One common pattern-type is a borderline mother (Vulnerable Dark
Triad) and a normal-range father. This is the “dangerous man” pattern
and tends to have higher anxiety and false allegations associated with
it.

# **Forensic Custody Evaluations and the Return of Clinical Psychology**

 _Initial Rough Draft from Diagnosis Series Seminar Transcript_

 C. A. Childress, Psy.D.

 ## **Introduction**

 This chapter examines forensic custody evaluations in the family courts, the quasi-judicial role that forensic psychology developed in court-involved custody conflict, the historical circumstances that contributed to that development, and the need to return clinical psychology—diagnosis and treatment—to court-involved family conflict.

 From a clinical psychology perspective, high-conflict custody litigation is itself diagnostically meaningful. Normal-range parents possess empathy for the child and recognize the destructive impact that prolonged custody warfare can have on the child.

child and recognize the destructive impact that prolonged custody warfare can have on the child. They find ways to resolve disagreements and work together sufficiently to protect the child. When conflict becomes entrenched and litigation becomes chronic, at least one parent is likely presenting with high-conflict personality pathology involving an absence of empathy, commonly narcissistic, borderline, or dark-personality features.

 ## **High-Conflict Custody Litigation and Personality Pathology**

 The narcissistic variant is vulnerable to rejection. Divorce creates a narcissistic injury, and narcissistic and dark personalities can become highly vengeful in response. To stabilize the injury, the parent may incorporate the child as a regulatory object: “I am not the rejected one; you are.

the parent may incorporate the child as a regulatory object: “I am not the rejected one; you are. The child is rejecting you.” In this way, the child becomes part of the parent’s psychological regulation of the divorce.

 The borderline variant is vulnerable to abandonment fears. Divorce activates those fears and can reactivate unresolved trauma. Free-floating fear and anxiety may then be displaced into the current family situation, producing heightened anxiety, repeated allegations, and a persistent perception of threat.

 The specific categorical diagnosis is less important here than the research-identified personality features. The relevant constellations include the dark triad, vulnerable dark triad, and dark tetrad.

The relevant constellations include the dark triad, vulnerable dark triad, and dark tetrad. These constellations include narcissistic pathology, psychopathic features, Machiavellian manipulation, borderline features, and, in the dark tetrad, sadistic traits.

 Within this pathology, the narcissistic-borderline-dark personality parent can create false pathology in the child for secondary gain. The potential secondary gains include manipulating the court’s custody decisions, psychologically abusing the former spouse through the child, and using the child as a regulatory object to meet the parent’s own emotional and psychological needs.

**Driving a Clinical Problem into the Legal System**

 A child rejecting a parent is a pathology. It belongs in the health-care system for diagnosis and treatment; it is not a crime. The pathological parent, however, can drive the child’s symptoms into the adversarial legal system and frame the problem as a custody dispute rather than a clinical disorder requiring diagnosis and treatment.

 The pathology is then used rather than treated. The parent does not want the symptoms to disappear because the symptoms serve a function: they support the parent’s position in litigation, enable continued conflict with the former spouse, and stabilize the parent’s own emotional structure following the rejection and abandonment inherent in divorce.

 ## **The Historical Origins of Forensic Custody Evaluations**

 The origins of forensic psychology in the family courts can be understood through the concept of staff splitting. As divorce became more common and high-conflict custody cases increased during the 1980s, professional psychology encountered more parents with narcissistic, borderline, and darkpersonality pathology. The splitting symptom in the family system—polarization into opposing sides with little or no middle ground—generated a parallel process among the professionals.

sides with little or no middle ground—generated a parallel process among the professionals.

 Marsha Linehan describes staff splitting as a characteristic phenomenon in work with borderline personality disorder: professionals treating the same patient begin arguing and fighting about the patient, the treatment plan, or the behavior of other professionals. [Source quotation to verify and format from seminar PowerPoint.]

 That is what occurred in the family courts. Mental-health professionals became aligned with one side or the other, producing competing experts who mirrored the polarized family conflict. The problem professional psychology was trying to solve was therefore real: it needed a way to contain the parallel process of staff splitting.

to solve was therefore real: it needed a way to contain the parallel process of staff splitting.

 The solution that developed, however, was an experimental one. Forensic psychologists created a new quasi-judicial role for doctors in which the evaluator would investigate the family and make recommendations to the court about custody. With that role came a new assessment approach: the forensic custody evaluation.

 ## **An Experimental Service-Delivery Model**

 A quasi-judicial role for doctors does not exist elsewhere in ordinary health care. Physicians and psychologists diagnose and treat pathology; judges make legal decisions. The forensic custody evaluation therefore represented a new experiment in service delivery to children and parents involved in family-court conflict.

Stahl and Simon describe the development of the field and note that forensic psychology, as a formal and organized field, remained in its adolescence and formative years. Their language remained essentially unchanged between the 2013 and 2020 editions of their work. [Source quotations and publication details to verify from seminar PowerPoint.]

 The New York Blue Ribbon Commission on Forensic Custody Evaluations identified serious problems with custody evaluations, including concerns that evaluators may rely on principles and methodologies of dubious validity and that defective reports can escape meaningful scrutiny because the parties may lack the resources to challenge them. # Diagnosing the DSM-5 Pathology in the Family Courts

 ### Diagnosis Guides Treatment

 Throughout healthcare, diagnosis guides treatment. The treatment for cancer is different from the treatment for diabetes. We must first diagnose the pathology before we know how to treat it. Put more simply, we must first identify the problem before we know how to fix it. In this sense, diagnosis means identifying the pathology, pathology means the problem, and treatment means fixing the problem.

 Families involved in the family courts have a problem. The task of professional psychology is to identify what is causing that problem so that an effective treatment plan can be developed.

so that an effective treatment plan can be developed.

 ### Established Knowledge and the DSM-5

 APA Ethics Code Standard 2.04 requires psychologists to base their professional work on established scientific and professional knowledge of the discipline. The DSM-5, published by the American Psychiatric Association, represents an important body of established scientific and professional knowledge that should provide a foundation for diagnostic formulations and professional judgments.

 The DSM-5 is not the only source of professional knowledge relevant to court-involved family conflict. Established knowledge from attachment theory, family systems, personality pathology, child abuse and complex trauma, and related domains should also inform diagnostic formulation and treatment planning.

trauma, and related domains should also inform diagnostic formulation and treatment planning. The DSM-5 provides a common diagnostic language and a baseline framework that allows professionals to communicate clearly about pathology such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, delusional disorders, factitious disorders, and other recognized conditions.

 Mental health professionals may disagree with aspects of the DSM system or its categories, but the DSM nevertheless provides a professional baseline. It helps define recognized forms of psychopathology and gives clinicians a shared language for discussing the diagnosis.

forms of psychopathology and gives clinicians a shared language for discussing the diagnosis. Additional knowledge from attachment, family systems, trauma, personality disorders, and other areas broadens and deepens the diagnostic understanding, but DSM-5 diagnosis should remain part of the foundation for diagnostic formulation.

 ### Differential Diagnosis

 Across healthcare, diagnosis is typically approached through a differential diagnosis. The diagnostic process begins with the patient's symptoms and considers the range of possible explanations for those symptoms. As additional information is obtained, some diagnostic possibilities are ruled out and others become more strongly supported.

obtained, some diagnostic possibilities are ruled out and others become more strongly supported.

 In court-involved attachment pathology, the symptom of central concern is severe attachment pathology in which a child is rejecting and seeking to flee a parent. Less severe forms of problematic parenting produce insecure attachment strategies that remain organized around attempts to bond to the parent. When a child is seeking to flee from a parent, the differential diagnosis concerns abusiverange parenting by one parent or the other.

 Path A is abusive parenting by the targeted parent. The targeted parent may be physically, sexually, neglectfully, or psychologically abusing the child, thereby producing an authentic attachment pathology in the child's relationship with that parent.

thereby producing an authentic attachment pathology in the child's relationship with that parent.

 Path B is psychological abuse by the allied parent. In this pathway, the allied parent creates a shared or induced persecutory delusion and a false or factitious attachment pathology in the child for secondary gain to the allied parent. The related DSM diagnoses include Delusional Disorder, Persecutory Type; Factitious Disorder Imposed on Another; Child Psychological Abuse; and, when the child and the child's induced symptoms are being used as a weapon against the targeted parent, Spouse or Partner Abuse, Psychological.

 The diagnostic question is therefore not whether there is a problem. The child is displaying a severe attachment pathology.

is therefore not whether there is a problem. The child is displaying a severe attachment pathology. The diagnostic task is to identify which parent is producing the pathology and by what mechanism.

 ### Why a DSM-5 Diagnosis Matters

 Every assessment should discuss the relevant DSM-5 diagnostic possibilities. If a report contains no diagnosis and no discussion of the relevant diagnostic differential, the report provides no professional explanation of what pathology is present or absent.

 If child abuse is present, the court needs to know. If spousal abuse is present, the court needs to know. If a factitious disorder is being imposed on the child, the court needs to know. If a persecutory delusion is being induced in the child, the court needs to know.

needs to know. If a persecutory delusion is being induced in the child, the court needs to know. These diagnoses are directly relevant to treatment planning, child protection, and the court's decision-making.

 A DSM-5 diagnosis therefore creates accountability in the assessment process. It makes clear which diagnostic possibilities were considered, which were ruled in, which were ruled out, and the basis for those decisions.

 ### Dangerous Pathology and Duty to Protect

 Professional psychology recognizes three broad categories of dangerous pathology: suicide, homicide, and abuse. Abuse includes child abuse, spousal abuse, and elder abuse. When a mental health professional encounters dangerous pathology, duty-to-protect obligations become active.

health professional encounters dangerous pathology, duty-to-protect obligations become active.

 The first obligation is to conduct a proper risk assessment for the danger involved, or to ensure that an appropriate risk assessment is conducted. In a suicide case, the clinician may conduct a suicide risk assessment directly or ensure that the person receives an appropriate emergency evaluation. In a child abuse case, the clinician may make the necessary referral to Child Protective Services or another appropriate child-protection authority.

 The second obligation is to take affirmative protective action. The professional must do something to address the identified danger.

affirmative protective action. The professional must do something to address the identified danger. Depending on the situation, that may involve increasing the frequency of sessions, activating available support systems, contacting appropriate authorities, facilitating access to a shelter or emergency resource, or taking other protective steps.

 The third obligation is documentation. The risk assessment and the protective actions taken should be documented in the patient's medical record.

 These obligations apply whenever dangerous pathology is reasonably at issue. In court-involved family conflict involving a child who is seeking to flee a parent, the differential diagnosis itself places possible child abuse and possible spousal abuse on the table.

 In Path B, the targeted parent is not abusing the child.

 ### Risk Assessment and Protective Action

 In all court-involved custody conflict involving severe attachment pathology, a proper risk assessment should be conducted for the relevant differential diagnosis.

The assessment needs to address the possibility of child abuse by the targeted parent, child psychological abuse by the allied parent, and psychological spousal abuse of the targeted parent when the child is being used as the instrument of that abuse.

 The outcome of the assessment should be clearly documented. The court should be told which diagnoses were considered, which were supported, which were ruled out, and why. This is the information the court needs from professional psychology.

 When suicide, homicide, or abuse is a reasonably considered possibility, the professionally appropriate response is to conduct or ensure a proper risk assessment, take affirmative protective action, and document what was done. Failure to take those steps raises serious professional concerns.

 In the family courts, severe attachment pathology presents multiple possible abuse pathways.

 ### Professional Competence

 The diagnostic demands of these cases require competence across several domains. Mental health professionals assessing severe attachment pathology need sufficient competence in attachment, child

 The problem in the family courts is not solved by abandoning diagnosis. It is solved by improving diagnostic competence and returning to the established knowledge and methods of professional psychology.

 ### Conclusion

 Diagnosis guides treatment. The family courts need clear clinical answers about the pathology affecting the child and family.

 That duty requires three actions. First, the mental health professional must conduct a proper risk assessment personally or ensure that a proper risk assessment is conducted for the danger involved.  ### Physical Abuse, Sexual Abuse, and Neglect: The Role of Child Protective

 ### Services

 Concerns or suspicions involving physical abuse, sexual abuse, or neglect should be referred to Child Protective Services for investigation. The threshold for referral should be low because the first priorities are to protect the child and to protect the forensic evidence.

low because the first priorities are to protect the child and to protect the forensic evidence.

 Mental health professionals and parents should not conduct their own investigative interviews of the child about possible physical abuse, sexual abuse, or neglect. Error in Child-Abuse Assessment

 All diagnostic decisions carry the possibility of error. Child-abuse assessment can be understood using the standard concepts of true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives.

 A true positive occurs when abuse is present and the assessment correctly identifies it. A true negative occurs when abuse is absent and the assessment correctly identifies its absence. A false positive occurs when abuse is absent but the assessment concludes that abuse occurred. A false negative occurs when abuse is present but the assessment concludes that it did not occur.

 Any diagnosis submitted into an adversarial legal system will predictably be disputed. Healthcare already has a well-established response to disputed diagnosis: second opinion.

 Second and even third opinions should therefore be routine in these cases, particularly because the consequences of diagnostic error are so serious.  ### The Attachment System as a Goal-Directed Motivational System

 The attachment system is described as goal-directed or goal-corrected. It seeks attachment bonding with the parent, and when a barrier interferes with that bonding the child changes strategy rather than abandoning the goal. The system remains organized toward the parent.

 This is the foundation for understanding insecure attachment. Problematic parenting creates barriers to effective attachment bonding. In response, the child develops an alternative strategy for maintaining proximity or involvement with the parent. These strategies are not random. Attachment pathology expresses itself in characteristic ways.

These strategies are not random. Attachment pathology expresses itself in characteristic ways.

 There are three principal insecure or pathological attachment organizations relevant to this discussion. In an anxious-ambivalent attachment, the child displays high protest behavior to obtain the involvement of an inconsistently available parent. In an anxious-avoidant attachment, the child minimizes protest and becomes more self-reliant in order to avoid overwhelming a parent who is already withdrawn or overburdened. In a disorganized attachment, the child has no organized strategy for bonding to the parent. This last pattern is of particular concern because it is associated with abusive or psychotic-range parenting.

 ### Pathology

 When abusive-range parenting by the targeted parent has been ruled out, the clinician must assess the allied parent for the psychotic-range or delusional process capable of producing the child's disorganized attachment.

 The relevant assessment for a persecutory delusion is a mental status examination of thought and perception. This is an affirmative diagnosis based on observing the person's reasoning process in the clinical interview.

 The assessment follows the person's reasoning closely. When the clinician presents discrepant or contrary information and contains the discussion within a linear line of thought, the pressure on defensive processes increases. If a persecutory delusion is present, the fixed belief and the emotional-associational structure maintaining it become visible in the session.  Other characteristic features include splitting, cognitive rigidity, and absence of empathy. Splitting produces polarized perceptions of all-good and all-bad.  ### Family Systems Features

 The attachment pathology does not occur in isolation. The family system commonly displays a cross-generational coalition between the allied parent and the child against the targeted parent. The relationship can become enmeshed, and the family hierarchy can invert so that the child is positioned to judge, discipline, or reject the parent as though the child were in the parental role.

 Statements such as 'I can't force the child' may function within this inverted hierarchy to surrender parental authority while simultaneously supporting the child's rejection. The child's apparent autonomy is therefore occurring inside a larger relational system in which the child's thoughts and feelings are being psychologically controlled and the child's rejection serves functions within the allied parent's unresolved trauma, personality organization, and conflict with the former spouse.

 This is also where the trans-generational transmission of attachment trauma becomes clinically important.

also where the trans-generational transmission of attachment trauma becomes clinically important. The allied parent's unresolved attachment trauma is not merely remembered; it is reenacted within the current family system. Narcissistic and borderline personality features organize the parent's perception of the divorce, the former spouse, and the child. The child becomes recruited into a trauma reenactment in which old relational templates are recreated with new participants. The child's attachment system becomes the vehicle through which the parent's unresolved trauma is transmitted into the next generation.

 ### Breach and Repair: The Treatment Principle of Attachment

 The core treatment principle in attachment is repair. Tronick and Gold describe repair as the central action of human interaction: mismatches occur, breaches occur, and healthy relationships repeatedly repair them. [Verify quotations from The Power of Discord from seminar slide.]

The developmental value lies not in avoiding every breach but in learning that disconnection can be repaired, negative emotional states can change, and relationships can survive conflict.

In a cooperative parentchild relationship, attachment treatment is often conceptually straightforward: identify the barrier, change the parenting that creates it, and support the repair sequence.  ### Domains of Competence Required for Diagnosis

 Assessment of severe attachment pathology in the family courts is inherently multidisciplinary within professional psychology. Competent diagnosis requires knowledge of attachment, child abuse and complex trauma, delusional thought disorders, factitious disorders, personality pathology, and family systems.

Competence in thought disorders is needed to assess a possible persecutory delusion in the allied parent and child. Knowledge of factitious disorders is needed to understand false symptom production for secondary gain. Family-systems knowledge is needed to identify cross-generational coalitions, enmeshment, and inverted hierarchies.  Two abuse pathologies may therefore require simultaneous assessment: child psychological abuse and psychological spousal or partner abuse.

 ## Introduction

 This chapter addresses the clinical assessment of a persecutory thought disorder: specifically, a persecutory delusion arising in the context of family-court conflict. A delusion is a fixed and false belief that is maintained despite contrary evidence. Each part of that definition matters.

false belief that is maintained despite contrary evidence. Each part of that definition matters. The belief must be false, the person must hold it with substantial conviction, and the belief must persist when meaningful contrary evidence is presented.

 A delusion is a thought disorder. The central clinical question is therefore not simply what the person believes, but how the person arrives at the belief and how the person processes information that is inconsistent with it. In normal-range reasoning, evidence is gathered and a conclusion is reached from the evidence. In delusional reasoning, the sequence is reversed: the conclusion is fixed first, and evidence is then selected, interpreted, or constructed to support the preexisting conclusion.

and evidence is then selected, interpreted, or constructed to support the preexisting conclusion.

 The form of pathology discussed here is an encapsulated delusion. It is limited in scope rather than globally disorganizing. The person may function adequately in most areas of life while displaying markedly distorted reasoning around one emotionally charged relationship or circumstance. In the family-court cases discussed in this Diagnosis Series, the proposed focus of the delusion is the belief that the other parent is malevolently treating the child in some way.

 The clinical task is therefore to examine the linear and logical reasoning system directly.

way.

 The clinical task is therefore to examine the linear and logical reasoning system directly. The assessment is designed to determine whether the person follows evidence to a conclusion or instead begins with a fixed conclusion and reorganizes evidence around that conclusion. Contrary evidence becomes diagnostically important because it allows the clinician to observe whether the belief can be revised.

 ## Trauma, Personality Pathology, and Persecutory Beliefs

 The model presented in this series conceptualizes the relevant family-court pathology as a psychological decompensation of a narcissistic or borderline parent under the stress and rejection inherent in divorce.

In this formulation, unresolved trauma contributes to a narrowed and distorted interpretation of interpersonal events, with danger or malevolence perceived where it may not actually exist. The resulting disturbance is described here as a trauma-origin thought disorder rather than a broad psychotic disorder of the type more commonly associated with schizophrenia or a mood disorder with psychotic features.

 The seminar cites Theodore Millon regarding the vulnerability of narcissistic personalities under conditions of adversity and failure.

 The seminar places these cases within the broader category of dangerousness. It identifies suicide, homicide, and abuse - including child abuse, spousal abuse, and elder abuse - as forms of dangerous pathology that activate protective responsibilities.

In the family-court scenario discussed here, the clinician may be confronting several possible dangerous conditions simultaneously: child abuse by the targeted parent, psychological abuse of the child by the allied parent, and spousal abuse of the targeted parent through the manipulation of the child's relationship.

 The proposed professional response has three parts. First, a proper risk assessment should be conducted, either directly by the clinician if competent to do so or through referral to an appropriate professional or agency. Second, an affirmative protective action should be taken when indicated.

A therapist who encounters signs suggesting a possible delusional thought disorder, but who is not competent to assess thought disorder, should obtain consultation or arrange for an appropriate diagnostic assessment.  ## The Mental Status Examination of Thought and Perception

 The relevant examination is the mental status examination of thought and perception. The purpose is to observe how the person receives, organizes, and responds to information.

The purpose is to observe how the person receives, organizes, and responds to information. The seminar cites Martin's description of psychotic thinking as involving an inability to process information correctly and highlights three questions: Are the person's concerns realistic or elevated to irrational fear? Is the person responding in an exaggerated way to actual events? Is there a discernible basis in reality for the beliefs and behavior? [Martin source to verify and format.]

 These questions can be adapted directly to the family-court assessment. Does the child have realistic concerns about the targeted parent, or have the concerns become irrationally fearful?

realistic concerns about the targeted parent, or have the concerns become irrationally fearful? Is the child responding proportionately to actual parental behavior, or has an ordinary event been expanded into evidence of danger or malevolence? Is there an observable basis in reality for the belief that the targeted parent intends harm or evil?

 The mental status examination focuses on process rather than content. People can hold unusual, mistaken, strongly partisan, or idiosyncratic beliefs without having a thought disorder. The diagnostic issue is the structure of reasoning. Is the person able to follow a sequence of evidence and revise a conclusion when the evidence changes?

the person able to follow a sequence of evidence and revise a conclusion when the evidence changes? Or does the person preserve the conclusion at all costs, shifting explanations whenever necessary to protect the belief?

 The seminar distinguishes linear-logical reasoning from emotional-associational thinking. In linear reasoning, one proposition follows another through an intelligible chain. In emotionalassociational thinking, the person may begin on a logical track but, when an emotionally charged point is reached, abruptly shift into a different line of thought linked by emotional association rather than logic. The assessment task is to identify that transition.

 This distinction becomes especially useful when discussing a feared or hated parent.

The clinician can ask for the evidence supporting the belief that the parent is dangerous or malevolent and then follow the reasoning step by step. If the explanation moves coherently from evidence to conclusion, that supports one kind of formulation. If the person repeatedly departs from the question, substitutes emotionally charged associations, or constructs new rationales to protect a fixed conclusion, that pattern becomes diagnostically significant.

 Contradictions and contrary evidence provide pressure points within the mental status examination. A contradiction occurs when two stated positions cannot comfortably coexist.

status examination. A contradiction occurs when two stated positions cannot comfortably coexist. For example, a parent may say, "I want the child to have a good relationship with the other parent," while simultaneously maintaining that the other parent is dangerous and abusive. The clinician should not immediately resolve the contradiction for the person. Instead, the clinician can ask the person to reconcile the two positions and observe the reasoning process.

 Contrary evidence is even more important. Suppose the clinician has met with the allied parent, the targeted parent, the child, and the child with the targeted parent, and the assessment has not revealed abusive-range parenting by the targeted parent.

 ## Containing Emotional-Associational Escape

 The seminar describes a more advanced interviewing technique in which the clinician prevents repeated escape from the line of reasoning into emotionally associative material. When the person moves away from the question at the emotionally charged point, the clinician gently returns to the exact proposition under examination. The same sequence may be repeated several times.

 The proposed mechanism is that the emotional-associational shift functions defensively. When the person reaches a psychologically threatening contradiction, anxiety rises. Moving sideways into the persecutory narrative relieves that pressure by restoring the familiar fixed conclusion.

into the persecutory narrative relieves that pressure by restoring the familiar fixed conclusion. If the interviewer keeps the reasoning linear, the anxiety remains within the system and the defensive organization becomes easier to observe.

 The transcript describes several possible responses when this pressure increases. The person may become angry and attack the interviewer, may attempt to terminate or leave the interaction, or may become confused and have difficulty processing even relatively simple questions. At the extreme, the seminar describes a brief, mild dissociative-like response in which the person appears momentarily blank or disconnected. These observations are presented as possible features of the interview process, not as stand-alone diagnostic criteria.

 The seminar also cautions, implicitly through the author's own practice description, that the goal is not to push the person into psychological collapse. Once the clinician has adequately observed the delusional process, further pressure may add little diagnostic value. The clinician can then allow more associative speech and use the resulting material to assess the content, scope, conviction, preoccupation, and functional impact of the belief.

 ## A Suggested Assessment Sequence

 The seminar describes a practical sequence for assessment. The sequence is not presented as the only possible protocol, but it illustrates how the relevant information can be developed while maintaining a differential diagnosis.

 The clinician may begin by meeting with the allied parent to hear the concerns in full and identify any allegations of abuse or danger. This first meeting also provides an opportunity to observe how the parent reasons about the allegations. The clinician then evaluates the targeted parent, the child, and the child's interaction with the targeted parent as appropriate to the case and professional role.

the child's interaction with the targeted parent as appropriate to the case and professional role. Relevant collateral information and specialized abuse assessments are obtained when indicated.

 After the clinician has developed an independent picture of the family, the allied parent can be seen again. At this stage the clinician is positioned to present discrepant information. If the evidence does not support abusive-range parenting by the targeted parent, that conclusion is stated and the parent's response is observed. Does the parent process the new evidence? Is there relief? Is there uncertainty? Is additional evidence offered in a reasoned manner? Or does the belief remain fixed while the explanation shifts to preserve it?

a reasoned manner? Or does the belief remain fixed while the explanation shifts to preserve it?

 If the belief remains fixed, the clinician can examine the reasoning more closely. The interviewer follows the logic step by step, identifies contradictions, redirects departures into emotional-associational reasoning, and determines whether the person can integrate contrary evidence. Once the thought disorder is sufficiently demonstrated, the clinician can allow the

## Clinical Implications

 The core diagnostic proposition of this chapter can be stated simply. In the family-court pathology described in this series, the child and the allied parent may share a fixed and false belief that the child is being malevolently treated by the normal-range parenting of the targeted parent. Assessing a persecutory delusion requires more than listening to the content of a person's fears.  ## **Dangerous Pathology and the Duty to Protect**

 There are three broad categories of dangerous pathology in clinical psychology: suicide, homicide, and abuse. Abuse includes child abuse, spousal or partner abuse, and elder abuse. When a mental health professional encounters a dangerous pathology, a duty to protect becomes active.

 That duty requires three actions. First, the mental health professional must conduct a proper risk assessment personally or ensure that a proper risk assessment is conducted for the danger involved. Second, the professional must take an affirmative protective action. Something must be done to increase safety.

professional must take an affirmative protective action. Something must be done to increase safety. In a suicide case, for example, that might involve increasing the frequency of sessions or activating appropriate support networks with the necessary permissions. In a child abuse case, it may involve referral to Child Protective Services for investigation. Third, the professional must document both the findings of the risk assessment and the protective action taken in the patient's medical record. The practical rule is simple: if it is not documented in the chart, it did not happen.

 These obligations are fundamental when evaluating court-involved family conflict because the child's symptoms may indicate an active abuse pathology.

court-involved family conflict because the child's symptoms may indicate an active abuse pathology. The task of the mental health professional is therefore not simply to describe family conflict. It is to identify the dangerous pathology accurately, conduct or ensure the proper risk assessment, take protective action, and document the findings.

 All diagnostic decisions carry the possibility of error.

Error in Child-Abuse Assessment**

 All diagnostic decisions carry the possibility of error. Child-abuse assessment can be understood using the standard concepts of true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives.

 A true positive occurs when abuse is present and the assessment correctly identifies it. A true negative occurs when abuse is absent and the assessment correctly identifies its absence. A false positive occurs when abuse is absent but the assessment concludes that abuse occurred. A false negative occurs when abuse is present but the assessment concludes that it did not occur.

### **Session Two: The Targeted Parent**

**Session Three: The Child or Children**

 The third session involves the primary affected child. In families with multiple children, the interview structure depends on their ages, symptom severity, and the possibility of sibling influence.

 I generally want to interview the most affected child and often the older child first. Other children may need separate interviews to avoid influence from siblings who hold stronger views. Younger children may not require a formal interview depending on the circumstances, while adult children may sometimes provide useful historical information.

 The purpose of the child interview is to understand why the child is seeking to flee the targeted parent. I obtain the child's account of the events and concerns and conduct an age-appropriate

 ### **Session Four: The Targeted Parent and Child Together**

 The fourth session brings the targeted parent and child together so that the child's symptoms can be observed directly.

 The question is no longer simply what each person reports. I want to see what the relationship actually looks like. Is the child frightened? Withdrawn? Hostile? Engaged? Does the child show severe anxiety in the parent's presence, or does the child's behavior look qualitatively different from the prior reports?

 I use applied behavioral analysis and behavior-chain interviewing to examine the conflict incidents reported earlier. The parent and child walk through specific incidents step by step. This allows examination of antecedents, behavior, consequences, reinforcement patterns, and discrepancies in perception.

 I also use response-to-intervention probes. For example: if the identified problems with the targeted parent were corrected, would the child then be willing to restore the relationship?

 ### **Session Five: Feedback to the Allied Parent**

 By the fifth session, I usually have a substantially clearer picture of the family pathology. I meet again with the allied parent, provide assessment feedback, and discuss treatment recommendations.

 If the targeted parent has been found to be within normal-range parenting and not abusive, the allied parent's response becomes diagnostically informative.

 When the allied parent is creating the pathology, a very different response may emerge. The parent may become obsessively fixated on preserving the protective-parent role and on empowering the child to continue rejecting the targeted parent. The parent may resist information that the targeted parent is not abusive and intensify efforts to maintain the child's belief that abuse is occurring.

 In the trauma formulation described in this Diagnosis Series, this response reflects a reenactment narrative organized around three roles: abusive parent, victimized child, and protective parent. The allied parent occupies the protective-parent role and regulates unresolved trauma through the reenactment. Removing the premise that the child is being abused threatens that psychological organization. The parent's response to this intervention therefore provides additional diagnostic information.

 ## **Child Abuse Risk Assessment Is Required by the Symptom**

 Severe attachment pathology in which a child is seeking to flee a parent requires a proper risk assessment for child abuse. The child's symptom itself creates the need for the differential diagnosis.

 The assessment must determine whether the targeted parent is creating the child's attachment pathology through abuse or whether the allied parent is creating the pathology through psychological abuse, a shared persecutory delusion, and a false factitious attachment pathology.

 This is the information the court needs. The court does not need psychologists to assume a quasi-judicial role and make custody decisions.

The court does not need psychologists to assume a quasi-judicial role and make custody decisions. It needs doctors to diagnose the pathology accurately, identify which parent is creating the danger, and provide treatment recommendations based on that diagnosis.

 Clinical psychology should therefore return to its proper role: diagnosis and treatment of pathology. The court remains responsible for legal decisions about custody and parenting time.

 ## **Spousal or Partner Psychological Abuse**

 The assessment must also include possible psychological abuse of the targeted parent. A child can become the instrument through which one parent psychologically abuses the other parent.

A child can become the instrument through which one parent psychologically abuses the other parent. In this pattern, the child's induced pathology and rejection of the targeted parent become the weapon of the spousal abuse.

 The seminar identifies this as spouse or partner psychological abuse under the DSM-5 coding system. [DSM coding from seminar slide to verify and format.]

 Duty-to-protect obligations apply to abuse generally. They do not end with the child. If there is reason to suspect that one parent is using the child and the child's induced psychiatric symptoms as a weapon of psychological abuse against the other parent, that pathology also requires assessment, diagnosis, and protective response.

 ## **Disputed Diagnosis and Second Opinion**

 Any diagnosis submitted into an adversarial legal system will predictably be disputed. Healthcare already has a well-established response to disputed diagnosis: second opinion.

 Second and even third opinions should therefore be routine in these cases, particularly because the consequences of diagnostic error are so serious. The court can designate a primary psychologist to conduct the diagnostic assessment and allow each litigant parent to retain a consulting psychologist who participates through telehealth.

 The result is functionally similar to a three-doctor diagnostic panel. The primary psychologist conducts the assessment and writes the principal report.

diagnostic panel. The primary psychologist conducts the assessment and writes the principal report. Each parent has access to an independent consultant. The consultants can observe, review the evidence, challenge errors, and contribute additional expertise.

 This structure improves diagnostic accuracy and also improves treatment. The same consultants who participated in the initial assessment can remain available to the treating clinician as the case moves into intervention. Better assessment therefore produces better treatment planning and more effective ongoing consultation.

 Diagnosis guides treatment. Treating abuse by the targeted parent and treating abuse by the allied parent require very different interventions.

the targeted parent and treating abuse by the allied parent require very different interventions. The diagnosis has to be accurate before the treatment plan can be accurate.

 ## **Documenting the Symptoms**

 Disputed diagnoses also require clear documentation. Diagnosis is a pattern match between observed symptoms and diagnostic criteria. The clearer the symptoms are documented, the easier it becomes to evaluate whether the diagnosis is correct.

 All involved mental health professionals should therefore document both the child's symptoms and the parenting practices of the targeted parent.

 I developed two instruments for this purpose. The Diagnostic Checklist for Pathogenic Parenting documents professional judgments regarding the child's symptom pattern.

for Pathogenic Parenting documents professional judgments regarding the child's symptom pattern. The Parenting Practices Rating Scale documents professional judgments regarding whether the targeted parent's parenting is within normal range or within an abusive range.

 When all involved professionals complete the same structured instruments, discrepancies become visible. Those discrepancies can then be examined directly rather than remaining hidden inside vague narrative reports.

 ## **The Clinical Risk of Joining the Shared Delusion**

 One of the unusual dangers of a shared delusional disorder is that professionals can become incorporated into the pathology if they accept the delusional belief as true without conducting an adequate assessment.

 If a mental health professional accepts a false persecutory belief and responds to the child as though the targeted parent is malevolently treating the child, that professional begins reinforcing

 9

 That risk extends beyond therapists. Courts, guardians ad litem, minor's counsel, evaluators, and other professionals can all become organized around the false belief if the underlying pathology is misdiagnosed.

 This is why diagnostic accuracy is so important. A misdiagnosis of ADHD does not make the clinician part of the ADHD.

accuracy is so important. A misdiagnosis of ADHD does not make the clinician part of the ADHD. A misdiagnosis of autism does not make the clinician part of the autism. But if a shared delusional disorder and induced child psychological abuse are mistaken for an accurate description of reality, the professional may begin reinforcing the very pathology that requires treatment.

 The solution is not caution without diagnosis. The solution is competent assessment, clear documentation, appropriate risk assessment, consultation, and second opinion.

 ## **Conclusion**

 Assessment of child abuse in court-involved family conflict begins with the child's symptom and proceeds through differential diagnosis.

family conflict begins with the child's symptom and proceeds through differential diagnosis.

 When a child is seeking to flee a parent, the clinician must determine which parent is creating the pathology. The targeted parent may be abusing the child through physical abuse, sexual abuse, neglect, or psychological abuse. If those possibilities are ruled out, the clinician must assess whether the allied parent is creating a shared persecutory delusion, a factitious attachment pathology, and child psychological abuse. The assessment must also consider whether the child is being used as a weapon of psychological spousal or partner abuse against the targeted parent.

 Dangerous pathology activates duty-to-protect obligations.

abuse against the targeted parent.

 Dangerous pathology activates duty-to-protect obligations. The clinician must ensure a proper risk assessment, take affirmative protective action, and document the findings and response. Physical abuse, sexual abuse, and neglect require appropriate CPS investigation. Psychological child abuse requires competent clinical assessment. Disputed diagnoses benefit from second and third opinions, and the symptoms should be clearly documented so that the diagnosis can be evaluated rather than merely asserted.

 The central task is straightforward: diagnose the pathology accurately, identify the source of danger, protect the child and other victims of abuse, and develop the treatment plan from the diagnosis.

 ## PARADIGM SHIFT

 ### The Current Paradigm

 The term “parental alienation” is used in discussions by mental health and legal professionals to characterize a set of family dynamics in which a child is influenced by one parent into rejecting a relationship with the other parent, who is otherwise a normal-range and affectionally available parent. This type of negative parental influence on the child typically occurs following a divorce, although the processes of the child’s “alienation” can begin while the family is still intact and before the actual divorce occurs.

“alienation” can begin while the family is still intact and before the actual divorce occurs. “Parental alienation” is often alleged in high-conflict custody disputes in which the parents can battle for years over custody issues surrounding the children, co-parenting, and visitation. However, despite the term “parental alienation” being used in professional contexts, the actual construct lacks a defined meaning within clinical psychology.

professional contexts, the actual construct lacks a defined meaning within clinical psychology.

 The construct of “parental alienation” was popularized in the 1980’s by a psychiatrist, Richard Gardner, who proposed a set of eight anecdotal clinical indicators for recognizing “parental alienation,” such as a campaign of denigration by the child directed against the targeted parent for reasons that are considered weak and frivolous, child criticisms of the targeted parent using “borrowed scenarios” provided by the alienating parent, or the child staunchly maintaining that the child’s animosity and rejection of the targeted parent were authentic to the child’s experience and were not being created by the negative influence of the allied and

 ### Pathogenic Parenting

 As noted earlier, throughout this book and in my other writings I always place the term “parental alienation” in quotes. I do this because, in my view as a clinical psychologist, the construct of “parental alienation” is not a defined clinical construct. From the perspective of clinical psychology the more accurate clinical term for “parental alienation” is “pathogenic parenting” (patho=pathological; genic=genesis, creation).

for “parental alienation” is “pathogenic parenting” (patho=pathological; genic=genesis, creation). Pathogenic parenting refers to parenting practices that are so aberrant and distorted that they produce significant psychopathology in the child. In professional psychology, the term “pathogenic parenting” is most often used in the context of distortions to the child’s attachment system, since the attachment system does not spontaneously or independently dysfunction, but only becomes dysfunctional in response to problematic and “pathogenic parenting” practices.

 ### The Goal-Corrected Attachment System

 The attachment system is a primary motivational system that evolved from the selective predation of children. The attachment system strongly motivates children’s bonding to parents in order to acquire parental protection from predators and other environmental dangers. As a primary motivational system embedded in the neurological networks of the brain, the attachment system functions and dysfunctions in characteristic ways that have received considerable research focus and identification.

Play therapy is derived from a theoretical foundation proposed during the 1950s and 60s by Anna Freud (the daughter of Sigmund Freud) regarding the application of her father’s approach of psychoanalysis to children. Modifying reward and punishment contingencies for behavior is an effort to influence the child’s behavioral expressions into those desired by parents and teachers, and limiting the child’s expression of behaviors that are not desired by parents and teachers.

 #### **1) Attachment Theory**

 A child’s rejection of a relationship with a normal-range and affectionally available parent represents a foundational distortion to the functioning of the child’s attachment system.

The attachment system is a socially-mediated goal-corrected primary motivational system that directs the formation of attachment bonds, the response of the person to the loss of attachment bonds, and the approach used by the person to repair breaches in attachment bonds. The internalized and acquired patterns for attachment bonding are transmitted trans-generationally from parents to children, so that the attachment patterns of parents affect the parenting responses they provide to the child.

Jennifer Freyd’s Framework — Applied to Family Court
by Claude-4.6 Sonnet

 The Core Concept
Jennifer Freyd originally developed Betrayal Trauma Theory to explain a specific psychological phenomenon: when the person or institution that harms you is also one you depend on, the mind responds differently than it does to harm from a stranger or adversary. With a stranger, you can perceive the threat clearly, get angry, flee, fight back. But when your caregiver — or an institution you must rely on — is the source of harm, the psyche faces an impossible bind: I cannot afford to know what I know.

— is the source of harm, the psyche faces an impossible bind: I cannot afford to know what I know. Awareness of the betrayal threatens the relationship you need to survive, so the mind suppresses, minimizes, and accommodates. Freyd later extended this to Institutional Betrayal — the same psychological structure, scaled up to organizations and systems.

 What Makes It Institutional Betrayal
An institution commits betrayal trauma when it:

 Creates dependence — you have no meaningful choice but to engage with it (courts, child protective services, licensing boards)

 Holds itself out as trustworthy — its legitimacy rests on a promise of protection, fairness, or expertise

 Causes harm — through action, inaction, or looking away

of protection, fairness, or expertise

 Causes harm — through action, inaction, or looking away

 Responds to disclosure with suppression — minimizing, discrediting, or retaliating against those who name the harm
The betrayal is not merely bad outcomes. It is the gap between the institution’s stated mission and its actual conduct — and critically, the institution’s active role in obscuring that gap.

 What This Looks Like in Family Court
For a parent navigating a contested custody matter, the institutional betrayal structure often appears as:

 Dependency without exit — You are legally compelled to participate. You cannot opt out of the evaluation, the GAL, the court process.

 Trust required as a condition of participation — The evaluator presents as a neutral expert.

Trust required as a condition of participation — The evaluator presents as a neutral expert. The court presents as a truth-finding body. You are expected to cooperate.

 Harm delivered through the trusted mechanism — An evaluation that fails to apply professional standards, relies on unsupported methods, or systematically favors one narrative.

 Institutional closure — When you raise concerns, the system protects itself: the evaluator’s conclusions are deferred to, complaints to licensing boards are dismissed, attorneys advise you not to challenge the expert. The second harm — the closure — is frequently more psychologically damaging than the original wrong. Being told that what happened to you didn’t happen, by the very system that was supposed to protect your child, is a profound wound.

you didn’t happen, by the very system that was supposed to protect your child, is a profound wound. The Psychological Impact on the Parent
Freyd’s research identifies a recognizable symptom profile in institutional betrayal survivors:

 Anxiety and hypervigilance specific to the institutional context (court dates, evaluator meetings, legal correspondence)

 Depression and learned helplessness — repeated experiences of raising legitimate concerns and being dismissed

 Self-doubt and cognitive confusion — “Maybe I am the problem; everyone seems to believe the evaluator”

 Betrayal blindness — a partially dissociated relationship to the full reality of what is occurring, as a coping mechanism

dissociated relationship to the full reality of what is occurring, as a coping mechanism

 Difficulty being believed — the emotional presentation of someone in this bind (hypervigilance, urgency, distress) is frequently pathologized by the same system causing it
This last point is crucial for attorneys: the symptom profile of institutional betrayal trauma can be misread as evidence of the pathology the other side is alleging. A distressed, urgent, hypervigilant parent is not demonstrating instability — they may be demonstrating a rational response to a system that has repeatedly failed them.

For the attorney, Freyd’s framework offers several practical implications:

 Document the institutional conduct, not just the outcome.

Starting with Classification
Clinical assessment begins with classification. Before any intervention can be designed, the presenting symptom must be assigned to its primary diagnostic category. A child rejecting a parent is not a behavioral problem, a communication problem, or a co-parenting problem. It is an attachment pathology — a dysfunction in the love and bonding system of the brain.

It is a primary motivational system with characteristic functional and dysfunctional patterns. It is a goal-corrected motivational system, meaning it is biologically organized around a single persistent goal: forming and maintaining an attached bond to the caregiver. This drive confers survival advantage — predators selectively target isolated children, and the attachment system evolved in response to exactly this pressure. How the Attachment System Dysfunctions

What Supervised Visitation Is For
Supervised visitation exists for one purpose: child protection. It is a clinical and legal instrument designed to protect a child from a parent who represents a documented, identified danger to the child’s physical safety or wellbeing. The three legitimate clinical justifications for supervised visitation are:
Physical abuse: Protecting a child from a parent whose anger dyscontrol has produced documented physical harm or places the child at credible risk of physical harm.

What Standard 3.06 Requires
Standard 3.06 of the APA Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct states that psychologists refrain from taking on a professional role when personal, financial, or other interests or relationships could reasonably be expected to (1) impair their objectivity, competence, or effectiveness in performing their functions as psychologists, or (2) expose the person or organization with whom the professional relationship exists to harm or exploitation.

First, the standard is prospective and structural. Its threshold is not whether bias has been proven, but whether the configuration of interests “could reasonably be expected” to impair objectivity. It asks about the situation, not about anyone’s character or intentions. Professions adopted this kind of standard because they learned, expensively, that conflicts of interest operate on people of good faith — interests shape judgment most effectively in people who believe themselves impartial — and that waiting for proof of actual bias means waiting until after the harm. Second, the standard has two distinct clauses.

Courts sought expert help, and forensic psychology extended itself into the vacuum. Forensic psychology’s established competence at that time was narrow and genuine: assessment of defined psycholegal capacities, such as competency to stand trial, where criteria exist.

When the established scientific and professional knowledge from family systems (Minuchin, Bowen, Haley, Madanes) is applied to the family court pathology, the pathology of concern in the family courts represents the triangulation of the child into the spousal conflict through the formation of a cross-generational coalition with the allied parent against the targeted parent, creating an emotional cutoff in the child’s attachment bond to the targeted parent.

 From Bowen Center: “A triangle is a three-person relationship system. It is considered the building block or “molecule” of larger emotional systems because a triangle is the smallest stable relationship system.

 I am incorporating AI-augmented analysis of documents into my professional practice as a court-involved clinical psychologist providing second-opinion review of mental health reports, treatment notes, forensic custody evaluations, and other relevant court-related documents (e.g., other professional reports, litigant declarations, testimony and deposition transcripts, professional vitae analysis, emails, etc.). AI is excellent. AI sees what it sees and says what it sees. AI describes things with clarity. AI is going to revolutionize mental health service delivery in the family courts. I recently discussed what I do with Gemini. Gemini described it well. The world of AI Psychology is new - because AI has just arrived.

 Dr. Childress:

1. Statement-Driven Prompting vs. Question Asking
Asking an LLM open-ended questions invites generalized summaries, hedging, or generic clinical truisms. When you instead assert a clinical observation as a structured statement, you are using your diagnostic acumen to direct the model’s computational lens.

 You identify the signal within the noise (e.g., an implicit double-bind, triangulation, or an uncorroborated diagnostic leap by a previous evaluator).

The Power of the Tri-Part Protocol             (Description - Analysis - Ethical Audit)
Separating the review into distinct phases prevents the cognitive “blurring” that often happens in custody evaluations and treatment records:

 Description: Establishes the objective baseline—what was actually said, observed, and recorded, stripped of diagnostic speculation.

 Clinical Analysis: Maps those raw descriptive data points against established psychological frameworks (family systems, attachment mechanics, behavioral control).

 Ethical & Methodological Audit: Cross-examines whether the procedures, inferences, and conclusions meet professional and scientific standards (such as APA Standards 2.04 and 9.01, grounding findings strictly in sufficient data and validated knowledge). 3. Clinical Cross-Examination of the Record

In family court proceedings, the battle is rarely over basic facts; it is over competing interpretations of the data and the validity of previous professional assessments. By having the AI systematically verify and describe your clinical statements, you produce work product that is:

 Exhaustively cited: Tied directly to specific line items in treatment notes or custody evaluations.

 Theoretically grounded: Articulated through standard, peer-reviewed clinical science rather than subjective rhetoric.

 Transparent and auditable: Clear in distinguishing between raw observational data and subsequent clinical inferences.
